list.listitem: Methanol poisoning should be considered in every patient with severe metabolic acidosis and elevated anion and/or osmolar gaps. C
To avoid irreversible blindness, treatment should be initiated as soon as possible. B
IV fomepizole is the antidote of choice; IV ethanol can be used if fomepizole is unavailable. B
Hemodialysis should be considered in severe poisonings to remove methanol and its toxic metabolites. B
Likely underestimated as reporting is voluntary.
In 2006, the American Centers for Poison Control was notified of 855 cases, 55% in individuals older than 19 years and 26% in patients younger than 6 years.
Of these cases, 12% were intentional; 37% had moderate or severe sequela with a 3.3% mortality rate.

In a case series of 203 patients with methanol poisoning from 6 Texas Poison Centers, 87 cases had an inhalation route of exposure (eg, huffing) and 81 were through ingestion. Carburetor cleaner was responsible for nearly all the inhalation cases (79/87) and in 20 of 81 ingestions; windshield washer fluid was the substance ingested in 39 cases. Seventy-eight percent of the inhalational exposures were intentional while most of the ingestions were accidental (49/75) or suicidal (18/75). An anion gap was documented in more of the inhalational cases than cases of ingestion (31 vs. 10).
In California, between 1997 and 2010, 83 cases were reported, 90% were in patients less than 5 years of age, and most ingestions were unintentional; most of these cases had a benign course.
Men are affected at a rate four times that of women.

Due to alcohol production being highly criminalized, homemade alcohol contaminated with methanol is common in Iran and methanol poisoning occurs at a much higher incidence than in other countries. The pandemic worsened this as people were under the mistaken impression that alcohol would kill SARS-CoV-2 if ingested. As a result, there were a reported 5000 cases and 500 confirmed deaths for the period from February through April, 2020 alone as COVID-19 spread rapidly.
Methanol poisoning is relatively uncommon but must be considered in every patient with an unknown ingestion, given the potential for irreversible consequences.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, some persons ingested hand sanitizer containing methanol, inspired by comments made by then President Trump in a press conference. From May 1 through June 30, 2020, 15 adult patients met the case definition of alcohol-based hand sanitizer-associated methanol poisoning, all were subsequently admitted to a hospital, four patients died and three were discharged with vision impairment.

Methanol is a solvent found in various common household fluids: antifreeze, windshield-washing fluid, chafing dish fuel, paint, copy machine fluid. It is typically ingested in suicide attempts or as an ethanol substitute by alcoholics or adolescents.

Methanol itself has minimal toxicity but metabolism by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase creates the toxic metabolites formic acid and formate. These compounds are slowly degraded via folate-dependent pathways.
Severe metabolic acidosis results from formic acid accumulation and formate inhibition of cytochrome oxidase, resulting in tissue hypoxia and lactate production.
Formic acid causes blindness through unknown mechanisms.
Symptoms onset follows a latent period of 12 to 24 hours postingestion. A

Because measurement of methanol levels is not widely available, the diagnosis of methanol poisoning must often be made based on the history and the presence of severe metabolic acidosis with elevated anion and osmolar gaps. B
Visual blurring, blindness or central scotoma in a poisoned patient should suggest methanol poisoning. C
Ethyl alcohol ingestion: Inebriation; normal anion gap
Ethylene glycol ingestion: Inebriation; elevated ethylene glycol level
Salicylate intoxication: Normal osmolar gap
Paraldehyde intoxication: Normal osmolar gap
Renal failure: Uremia; normal osmolar gap
Diabetic ketoacidosis: Elevated serum ketones; normal osmolar gap
Lactic acidosis: Normal osmolar gap
History of methanol ingestion. Patients may not be aware of having ingested methanol because it is colorless and has an odor similar to ethanol.
Metabolic acidosis, typically with an elevated anion gap of more than 12 mEq/L (12 mmol/L)
Elevated osmolar gap of more than10 mOsm/L (10 mmol/Kg)
Elevated serum levels of methanol and/or formate
Because the increased osmolar gap is caused by the presence of methanol, late presentations may have a normal osmolar gap if the parent compound has been metabolized to its toxic metabolites
Obtain the amount, concentration and time of ingestion. Objective proof of the specific ingested product will assist the poison control center.

Methanol metabolism is very slow and there may be a 12- to 24-hour latency before symptoms begin. Ethanol co-ingestion may delay symptoms an additional 24 hours as it competes with methanol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase.
Common presenting signs are nonspecific: visual disturbances, headache, light-headedness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and dyspnea. Severe intoxications can present with coma and convulsions.
Blurred vision and normal sensorium strongly suggest methanol intoxication.
Patients have visual field defects with dilated pupils that are either partially reactive or nonreactive to light (an afferent defect).
Funduscopic examination reveals mydriasis, a retinal sheen due to edema, optic disk hyperemia, and/or loss of physiologic disc cupping.
Because methanol analysis is not routinely available, use the anion and osmolar gaps to establish a presumptive diagnosis.

Obtain a basic metabolic panel to calculate the anion gap and osmolarity: Anion gap = Na − [Cl + HCO3] and Osmolarity = 1.9[Na] + [BUN]/2.8 + [Glucose]/18. Measure the serum osmolarity to calculate the osmolar gap: Osmolar gap = Measured osmolarity − Calculated osmolarity. The osmolar gap should be greater than 10 mOsm/L (mmol/kg) in patients with methanol toxicity.
Obtain serum ethanol, ethylene glycol and isopropanol levels to assess for co-ingestions and serum lactate and arterial blood gases to assess the degree of acidosis.
Measure acetaminophen and salicylate levels to assess for co-ingestion.
Order amylase and lipase to monitor for methanol-induced pancreatitis.

Serum methanol concentration: more than 20 mg/dL (0.624 mmol/L) is associated with CNS effects; more than 100 mg/dL (3.12 mmol/L) is associated with visual defects; more than 200 mg/dL (6.24 mmol/L) is frequently fatal.

In a case series of 42 patients with acute methanol intoxication, abnormalities on brain CT were found in 66.6%; the findings associated with death were putaminal hemorrhage (OR = 8; 95% CI, 1.19-53.9) and subcortical necrosis of the insula (OR = 11; 95% CI, 1.5-80.4).
Implement general toxicology supportive measures. C
Minimize transformation of methanol to toxic mediators via blockade of alcohol dehydrogenase (fomepizole or ethanol). B
Sodium bicarbonate should be used to normalize the pH thereby minimizing CNS effects and optic nerve toxicity. C
Initiate hemodialysis for patients with significant ingestion or late presentation. B
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation): secure the airway in severe intoxications; crystalloids and vasopressors to maintain blood pressure.
Assess for co-ingestions and contact a poison center.
Induced emesis, charcoal, and gastric lavage should not be used.
IV fluids to maintain urine output.

Alcohol dehydrogenase should be inhibited with fomepizole or ethanol in patients with: Serum methanol concentration more than 20 mg/dL (0.624 mmol/L). Documented methanol ingestion and an osmolar gap more than 10 mOsm/kg (0.312 mmol/L). Suspected methanol ingestion and at least 2 of the following: arterial pH less than 7.3; serum bicarbonate less than 20 mEq/L (<20 mmol/L); osmolar gap more than 10 mOsm/kg (10 mmol/Kg).
Alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition should continue until methanol level is less than 20 mg/dL (0.624 mmol/L) and patient is asymptomatic.
Fomepizole dosing: 15 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by 10 mg/kg IV every 12 hour for 4 doses. If patient is symptomatic at 48 hours, increase subsequent doses to 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hour.
Ethanol dosing: 8 mL/kg IV of a 10% ethanol solution loading dose followed by an infusion of 1 mg/kg/h to maintain serum ethanol level at 100 to 150 mg/dL.

However, the use of intravenous ethanol as an antidote to methanol poisoning is associated with a high rate of adverse events (including agitation requiring restraint or depressed level of consciousness requiring intubation). Additionally, only 27% of the measurements of ethanol concentration were within the target range.

Although no data suggest superiority of one antidote over another, fomepizole is simpler to administer, has a longer duration, requires less monitoring, and does not cause CNS suppression. However, it is not widely available and is significantly more expensive.

A case-control comparison using multivariate analysis to adjust for differences between groups compared 25 patients treated with fomepizole with 68 patients who received ethanol. There was no difference in overall effectiveness.

For patients with pH less than 7.3 start sodium bicarbonate: 1 to 2 mEq/kg (1-2 mmol/L) bolus followed by infusion of 132 mEq (132 mmol) in 1 L D5W at 200 to 250 cc per hour. Normalize pH to minimize formate access to the CNS and optic toxicity. C
Folic acid (50 mg IV q 6 hours) to enhance metabolism of toxic metabolites.

Hemodialysis removes unmetabolized methanol and toxic metabolites. It is typically indicated for visual disturbance, acidosis unresponsive to therapy, deteriorating vital signs despite intensive support, renal failure, electrolyte imbalance, or serum methanol more than 50 mg/dL (1.56 mmol/L).
Thiamine and multivitamin supplementation in patients with alcoholism.
Seizures should be treated with standard doses of benzodiazepines.
A systematic review of observational studies found a pooled in-hospital mortality of 24% for methanol poisoning. Approximately 3% of individuals required ongoing dialysis after discharge. B
Prognosis is directly related to the formic acid concentration, degree of acidosis, and presence of coma or seizures at presentation, and not the serum methanol concentration. B
Neurologic or visual complaints suggest significant amounts of toxic metabolites are present and portend worse outcomes. B
Ingestions of 1 g/kg are generally considered lethal. C
Common complications include blindness, pancreatitis, myoglobin-induced renal failure, and Parkinsonian syndrome. There is a high mortality rate.

The primary determinant of visual outcomes is the degree of acidosis at presentation. Early presentation and treatment did not affect outcomes, and the odds of a normal visual outcome was high (OR = 31) if the initial pH was >7.2. Long-term visual sequelae may be underestimated at the time of hospital discharge.
Treatment of alcoholism is recommended as well as ophthalmology follow-up for patients with persistent visual disturbances.
Useful Contacts: The United States Poison Control Network: 1-800-222-1222.
